name: Monasteries
tagline: Prayer halls, masks and butter lamps
summary: Sikkim has a gompa in almost every valley, from Dubdi (1701) above Yuksom to Rumtek, seat of the Karma Kagyu lineage in exile. We time visits for morning prayers and the mask-dance days of the Tibetan calendar, and we brief you on the etiquette before you step inside.
intro: Buddhism reached Sikkim with the Nyingma lamas who consecrated the first Chogyal at Yuksom in 1642. The monasteries that followed, Pemayangtse, Tashiding, Phodong, Rumtek, still run on ritual time: prayers at dawn, cham dances on fixed days of the lunar year.
Walk clockwise, ask before photographing inside a prayer hall, and keep your voice low. Mask-dance dates move with the Tibetan calendar each year, so check current status before you travel.

name: Lakes and passes
summary: High-altitude lakes and border passes are why most people come: Tsomgo at 3,753 m, Gurudongmar at about 5,183 m, Nathu La at 4,310 m. Every one needs a permit and a sensible ascent. We handle both.
intro: Sikkim's best-known sights sit above 3,500 m, inside protected or border areas. Permits are issued only through registered agents, often a day ahead, and some sites close on certain weekdays or after snow.
Altitude is the real cost of these trips. We sleep you lower than you visit, carry water and dry fruit, and turn back without argument if anyone feels unwell. Check current status before you travel.

name: Snow and winter
summary: Snow usually reaches Tsomgo, Nathu La, Zero Point, Lachung and the Silk Route between December and March. Roads close after heavy falls and reopen when the Army and BRO clear them, so winter trips need a flexible day.
intro: Gangtok rarely sees snow, but an hour above it the road to Tsomgo often turns white by late December. Lachung and Yumthang are snowbound for much of January and February, and Zero Point is snow from November to April most years.
We plan winter trips with a buffer day, a 4x4 where the road needs one, and rooms with heating. Road and pass status changes daily in winter: check current status before you travel.

name: Flowers and forests
summary: Sikkim's state tree is the rhododendron and its state flower the noble orchid. Barsey, Yumthang's Shingba sanctuary and the Goecha La trail turn red, pink and white from March to May. We plan around bloom, not calendars.
intro: Rhododendrons flower from about 1,800 m in March up to the alpine zone in late May, so one trip can follow the bloom uphill. Orchids are best in the lower valleys and at the orchid sanctuaries around Gangtok.
Bloom moves with the weather each year. We watch reports from the sanctuaries and tell you honestly if a week looks early or late.

name: Village homestays
tagline: Sleep in the house, eat in the kitchen
summary: Registered homestays in Dzongu, Kewzing, Okhrey, Uttarey, Zuluk and dozens of other villages, paid fairly and booked directly with families. The cheapest way to see Sikkim, and the way you learn the most.
intro: Sikkim has a wide network of registered rural homestays, many run by families and village committees. Rooms are simple and clean, meals are what the family cooks, and the money stays in the village.
Expect shared bathrooms in some houses, early dinners and quiet nights. Bring a torch, cash and patience with the hot water.

name: Honeymoons
summary: A room facing Kangchenjunga in Pelling, a snow day at Tsomgo, a slow evening on MG Marg. We plan Sikkim honeymoons with fewer hotel changes, at least two nights per stop, and one or two set pieces you will remember.
intro: Most Sikkim packages move every night. A honeymoon should not. We build around two or three bases and spend the extra on the room, not the mileage.
Snow, views and good rooms cost more from October to December and around the New Year. Book early for those weeks.

name: Family holidays
tagline: Short drives, warm rooms, no surprises
summary: Routes with drives under five hours, warm rooms, and altitude added slowly. North Sikkim does not allow children under 5 in its protected areas, so we plan around that and tell you before you book.
intro: Families travel better with fewer hotel changes and a rest day built in. We cap most drives at four or five hours and plan high sights as morning trips from a lower base.
Age rules matter here: children under 5 are not permitted in North Sikkim protected areas, and very high sights are hard on small children and older parents. Check current status before you travel.

name: Treks and walks
tagline: From village trails to Goecha La
summary: Day walks to Hanuman Tok and Tendong, the Hilley–Barsey rhododendron trail, the Monastery Trail in the west and the Dzongri–Goecha La trek into Khangchendzonga National Park. Graded by hours and height gained.
intro: You do not need to be a mountaineer to walk in Sikkim. Many trails link villages and monasteries with three to five hours on foot and a car waiting at the end.
The big treks need permits, a registered guide and fitness. We grade every walk by hours, height and terrain, and tell you plainly who it suits.

name: Food and tea
tagline: Momo, churpi, gundruk and Temi tea
summary: Sikkim cooks Bhutia, Lepcha and Nepali food side by side: momo and thukpa, phagshapa and sel roti, fermented gundruk and kinema, yak churpi. Add Temi's organic tea and a fully organic state since 2016.
intro: Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016. You taste it in the vegetables at Lal Bazaar, the buckwheat and the millet, and in Temi's tea.
The best meals are at home tables and small cafés, not hotel buffets. Tell us about allergies and diets when you enquire.

name: Festivals
summary: Losar, Losoong, Saga Dawa, Pang Lhabsol, Bumchu at Tashiding, Tendong Lho Rum Faat and the mask dances of each monastery. Most follow the Tibetan or lunar calendar, so dates move every year.
intro: Sikkim's festivals belong to its communities: Lepcha, Bhutia, Limbu and Nepali, Buddhist and Hindu. Many happen in monastery courtyards and village grounds, open to respectful visitors.
Dates shift with the moon. We confirm the year's dates with the monastery or organisers before we build the trip. Check current status before you travel.

name: Birds and wildlife
tagline: Red panda country and a long bird list
summary: The red panda is Sikkim's state animal and the blood pheasant its state bird. Kitam, Maenam, Fambong Lho, Kyongnosla and Khangchendzonga National Park hold most of what birders come for. Sightings are never promised.
intro: Sikkim packs subtropical forest, temperate oak and fir, and alpine meadow into one small state, which is why the bird list is so long. Early mornings and local guides matter more than any gear.
Red pandas are shy and rarely seen in the wild. We never promise wildlife, and we never use guides who bait or chase animals.

name: Photography
summary: Sunrise on Kangchenjunga from Pelling or Tashi View Point, the Zuluk loops at dawn, prayer flags at Tsomgo, Rumtek's courtyard in morning light. We plan for the hours that matter and the weather windows that open them.
intro: The mountain shows itself most reliably from October to December and on clear spring mornings. Afternoons cloud over in most seasons, so photography trips start early and rest in the middle of the day.
Drones need permission and are banned near border areas, monasteries and military sites. Ask before photographing people and inside prayer halls.

name: Crafts and culture
summary: The Directorate of Handicrafts and Handloom in Gangtok, Lepcha weaving in Dzongu, thangka painters, carpet weavers and woodcarvers. We take you to workshops and take no commission on what you buy.
intro: Sikkim's crafts come from its communities: Bhutia carpets and choktse folding tables, Lepcha cane work and weaving, Nepali metalwork and woodcarving. Many workshops welcome visitors.
Buy from the maker or a government emporium when you can. We do not take commission, so we have no reason to push you anywhere.

name: Offbeat Sikkim
summary: Okhrey, Hee Bermiok, Dzongu, Rolep, Kewzing, Uttarey and the new district of Soreng. Quieter roads, cheaper rooms, and places where you are a guest, not a number on a sightseeing list.
intro: Most Sikkim packages repeat the same six stops. A day's drive from any of them are villages with homestays, monasteries and views that see a fraction of the traffic.
Offbeat means simpler rooms, longer drives on smaller roads and fewer ATMs. It also means you meet people. Carry cash and keep a buffer day.
